El campo receptivo es la clave de por qu: The receptive field is the key to why these networks are deep. With $3\times3$ kernels, the first layer sees 3 pixels across; the second, 5; the third, 7. That is why a few layers are enough for the last one to see the whole image, and that is why the first layers learn edges and the last ones, complete shapes.

It is the property that defines a convolution, and it can be checked with [[av-convolucion|convolution]]'s formula: since the kernel is the same at every position, moving the signal before or after filtering it gives the same result.

A dense layer does not satisfy this, because each position has its own weights. A convolutional layer satisfies it by construction, and that is the whole invention.

La demostración de que esto funcionaba a: The demonstration that this worked at scale came with ImageNet, the database of millions of labelled images that Fei-Fei Li drove forward from 2007 and that nobody was asking her for: at the time it was thought that what was missing was better algorithms, not more data. Its annual competition became the field's thermometer, and in 2012 a convolutional network won by such a large margin over the classical methods that it reoriented the whole discipline within months. Today the same architecture reads number plates, classifies X-rays, detects defects on assembly lines and is what looks out through your phone's camera when it focuses on a face.
La frase que resume el tema, y que convi: The sentence that sums up the topic, and that is worth being able to repeat: a convolutional network is a dense network that shares weights, because an image does not change its meaning when it is shifted. Everything else is a consequence of that.
La idea no nació en informática sino en: The idea was not born in computing but in neurophysiology. In the sixties David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel discovered, by measuring neurons in a cat's visual cortex, that there were cells that responded to edges with a particular orientation in a small area of the visual field, and that others higher up combined those responses; it earned them the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1981. Kunihiko Fukushima built the Neocognitron in 1980 following that hierarchy. And Yann LeCun added at the end of the eighties what was missing, training the filters with backpropagation instead of designing them: his LeNet network read the postcodes of the US mail and the amounts on cheques long before anybody talked about deep learning.
